Description: We primarily AIM to answer two questions related to galaxy clusters, which are the largest bound objects to have formed in our universe. FIRST, what is the distribution of their three-dimensional triaxial shapes? this distribution is influenced BY cosmology, for instance the properties of dark matter, and therefore provides an incisive cosmological test. in addition, a precise knowledge of the shape distribution is important to maximizing the cosmological science reach of missions such AS erosita and euclid. second, what is the level of non-thermal pressure support within the gaseous intra-cluster medium (icm) that contains most of the galaxy cluster s baryons? the average non-thermal pressure fraction, and the intrinsic scatter about this average, are dictated BY a range of astrophysical processes such AS outbursts from active galactic nuclei and the shock-heating of infalling newly accreted material. our results will provide a better understanding of how these processes influence large scale structure formation, particularly in light of recent observational studies that find much lower non-thermal pressure fractions than seen in simulations. our analysis will focus on the 118 galaxy clusters in the XMM-heritage program. these objects were selected from the planck all-sky survey to provide two equal-size representative samples: a volume-limited sample spanning a wide mass range in the local universe and a mass-limited sample including the largest objects that have formed to date. highly uniform deep multi-probe data will be available for the entire sample, including x-ray spectroscopic imaging from XMM- newton, sunyaev-zel dovich (sz) effect maps from planck and additional ground-based facilities, and wide-field gravitational lensing (gl) data from subaru, cfht, and other facilities. the x-ray and sz data redundantly probe the icm thermodynamics and CAN thus be combined to measure the shape of the galaxy cluster along the line of sight. combined with plane-of-sky shape information from the imaging data, three-dimensional triaxial models CAN be constrained from the data. including this shape information, the gl data directly measure the total mass of the galaxy cluster, and thus the pressure required to offset gravity. the non-thermal pressure CAN be obtained from the difference between this value and the thermal pressure directly probed BY the x-ray and sz data. the unique combination of excellent multi-probe data and representative sample selection will allow us to robustly characterize the distribution of three-dimensional shapes and non-thermal pressure profiles within the galaxy cluster population. we will make extensive use of publicly available data from XMM-newton and planck to obtain novel scientific results, thus satisfying the primary intent of the ADAP program. in addition, we will directly address the goals described for two of the three focused programs within the NASA astrophysics division, physics of the cosmos (pcos) and Cosmic Origins (COR). we will directly constrain cosmology, and inform cosmological studies from missions such AS erosita, results that are perfectly aligned with the pcos program s AIM to  understand how the universe works . the COR program aims to  understand how the universe has changed from its initial simple state  into the current  magnificent universe  with  stars, galaxies, and planets . we will address this goal BY providing a better understanding of how the large scale structures in our universe form and evolve, including physical processes that are important to star formation.

Description: The purpose of large scale structure (lss) surveys, both space based such AS euclid and wfirst, and ground based, such AS desi and lsst, is to elucidate the questions of origins of structure in our universe and its contents. the primary goal of this proposal is to develop a new theoretical and numerical modeling of how to extract the cosmological information from the large scale structure observations BY these surveys. we propose to DO this in the context of a recently developed framework which holds the promise of extracting all the cosmological information optimally. the method starts with an exact bayesian probabilistic model for the cosmological parameters given the data, which is then solved through a process that combines elements of numerical optimization in high dimensions and analytic marginalization to find the best solution for cosmological parameters and their covariance matrix. we propose to apply this method both to weak lensing and galaxy clustering observations, AS well AS to datasets that combine both. we will investigate cosmological parameters and astrophysical nuisance parameters that are to be marginalized over. the methods will be developed using realistic simulations of both dark matter and of galaxies populated in the dark matter simulations, before being applied to REAL data. results of this study will provide new methods that may dramatically improve upon the existing methods and may be of direct and significant benefit to space and ground based lss missions.

Description: This proposal to NASA BY the california association for research in astronomy (CARA) dba w. m. keck observatory (WMKO) is for renewal of the cooperative agreement award for support of NASA missions and NASA scientific research at WMKO, which operates the world s two (2) largest steerable optical and infrared telescopes on the summit of maunakea on the island of hawaii. NASA utilizes one-sixth of the annual operation capability of WMKO, having invested one-sixth of the capital costs and one-sixth of the operations costs since circa 1996. there has been a wealth of scientific results coming from the DYNAMIC scientific relationship between NASA missions such AS hubble space telescope (hst), spitzer, kepler, k2, chandra, herschel, WISE, galex, voyager, galileo, deep impact, cassini, new horizons, and the keck observatory. we propose here to extend that productive relationship to future NASA missions jwst, TESS, wfirst, euclid, mars 2020, and other MIDEX, SMEX, discovery, and new frontiers missions. the link between NASA and WMKO is powerful. NASA s space based discoveries inform and are informed BY the findings of its ground based partner, the w. m. keck observatory. NASA related projects are proposed BY the us community to nexsci and are awarded observing time provided BY NASA. this has proven productive in the past. a PRIME example is when kepler discovered objects transiting stars, WMKO undertook key observations that established that the candidate exosolar planets were indeed valid exosolar planets, and measured their masses, leading to the achievement of one of NASA s level 1 science goals: making a census of planetary systems down to the level of earth-sized planets. when spitzer and hst both detected an object in the distant universe, WMKO delivered the exact redshift of 8.68, well within the region that was thought to be the dark age before reionization. the research program enabled BY the NASA/WMKO partnership maps directly to the astrophysical and planetary priorities of NASA: the origin and evolution of the universe, the processes for life on other planets, the processes of formation of stars, galaxies, and planets, and the content, origin, and evolution of the SOLAR system and the potential for life elsewhere. the scope of the astrophysics and planetary science is breathtaking, ranging from the birth of the universe and the development of stars and galaxies over cosmic time, to the search for life on planets around other stars, to the formation, evolution, and possibility of life on other planets in our own SOLAR system. the two 10-meter primary apertures, diverse instrument suite including adaptive optics and the superb location on maunakea make WMKO an extraordinarily powerful and unique facility for addressing the research areas described above. additionally, WMKO CAN react quickly to NASA mission needs, rearranging nights on short notice. the track record of discoveries BY scientists using the WMKO in conjunction with NASA missions over the last two (2) decades gives strong testimony to that CASE. the program corresponding to NASA s in-guide funding amount provides NASA one-sixth of WMKO operations support and, in collaboration with the NASA exoplanet science institute (nexsci), WMKO will continue its Keck Observatory Archive (KOA) activities. in addition, we submit here an over-guide that allows for the development of data reduction pipelines (drps) over a period of five (5) years, to speed the reduction of new data with improved tools and to ACCESS the information inherent in 25 years of  the keck sky  easily and efficiently for all users. this proposal consolidates all direct NASA support for WMKO into one award.
